--- title: "2.3 Linear Interaction Effects" --- > *"Interaction effects exist when the effect of one independent variable is contingent on the level of another independent variable. For example, does the effect of obtaining more education depend on whether someone is white or black? Does the effect of aging depend on whether someone is a man or a woman?"* ([Mize 2019 p.81](https://www.sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/)) - Interaction effects are also known as moderation (i.e., one IV moderates the effect of another IV) - Can allow the effect of one IV to vary across levels of another IV by including a product term of the two variables in the model - Multiply the two IVs together - Include the two original IVs *and* the product term in the model ## Interaction effect example and interpretation ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear (cda_gss.dta | GSS 1972-2021 CDA - Categorical Data Analysis | date created 202 > 3) . . regress occprest c.age##i.woman i.college Source | SS df MS Number of obs = 58,304 -------------+---------------------------------- F(4, 58299) = 4703.09 Model | 2777942.63 4 694485.657 Prob > F = 0.0000 Residual | 8608766.27 58,299 147.665762 R-squared = 0.2440 -------------+---------------------------------- Adj R-squared = 0.2439 Total | 11386708.9 58,303 195.302281 Root MSE = 12.152 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- occprest | Coefficient Std. err. t P>|t| [95% conf. interval] --------------+---------------------------------------------------------------- age | 0.072 0.004 16.316 0.000 0.063 0.081 | woman | Women | 2.365 0.290 8.146 0.000 1.796 2.934 | woman#c.age | Women | -0.055 0.006 -9.343 0.000 -0.067 -0.044 | college | College De.. | 16.392 0.121 135.948 0.000 16.156 16.628 _cons | 35.226 0.216 162.811 0.000 34.802 35.650 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- . est store opintmod . est table opintmod, /// > title("[2.3.a] Occupational prestige linear regression model" /// > "Interaction between age & gender") /// > b(%5.3f) star(.05 .01 .001) [2.3.a] Occupational prestige linear regression model Interaction between age & gender --------------------------- Variable | opintmod -------------+------------- age | 0.072*** | woman | Women | 2.365*** | woman#c.age | Women | -0.055*** | college | College D.. | 16.392*** _cons | 35.226*** --------------------------- Legend: * p<.05; ** p<.01; *** p<.001 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(haven) # import Stata data and labels library(dplyr) # data manipulation library(ggplot2) # graphs library(modelsummary) # regression tables library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects library(cleanplots) # graph scheme cleanplots_defaults() gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta") # Keep only model vars and drop any missing data on them gss <- gss[c("occprest", "age", "woman", "college")] gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ] # Treat binary variables as factors using their value labels gss <- gss |> mutate(woman = as_factor(woman), college = as_factor(college)) intmod <- lm(occprest ~ age * woman + college, data = gss) modelsummary(intmod, stars = c("*" = .05, "**" = .01, "***" = .001), title = "[2.3.a] Occupational prestige linear regression model: Interaction between age & gender") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} For linear additive effects, the coefficient on the product term tests whether there is an interactive relationship between the two IVs (i.e., whether the effect of one variable *depends on* the level of another variable). **This is only the case for linear additive effects** > *The effect of age on occupational prestige is different for men and women (interaction term p \< 0.001)* What is the effect of age for men? For women? Because "woman" is coded as 1, *β~age~* tells us the effect of age for men (when *woman* = 0). The effect of age for women = *β~age~* + *β~woman\ X\ age~* which is 0.072 -- 0.055 = 0.017. **Again, this is only the case for linear additive effects.** I generally go straight to plotting predictions with interactions ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . qui margins, at(age=(20(5)80) woman=(0 1)) . marginsplot, /// > title("[2.3.b] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age and G > ender", size(medium)) /// > subtitle("Interaction Term: Gender X Age") /// > ytitle("Occupational Prestige") /// > recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs14)) ylab(38(2)46) Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman ``` ![](fig/cda-02_03_b-interaction-1.png){width=80% fig-alt="Predicted occupational prestige by age for men and women: two straight lines that cross, with a steeper slope for men."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions(intmod, by = c("age", "woman"), newdata = datagrid(age = seq(20, 80, 5), woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(38, 46, 2), limits = c(38, 46)) + labs(title = "[2.3.b] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age and Gender", subtitle = "Interaction Term: Gender X Age", x = "Age", y = "Occupational Prestige") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-3-linear-interactions_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='Predicted occupational prestige by age for men and women: two straight lines that cross, with a steeper slope for men.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Marginal effects by levels of another variable - With linear effects, we can calculate the slope for each level of the nominal variable (here, *woman*) by adding the coefficients - But, the coefficients don't provide a significance test for the effect of *age* for woman=1 - Marginal effects straightforwardly provide this, without the need for mental math ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . est restore opintmod (results opintmod are active now) . mecompare age, by(woman) Predicting: Linear prediction Marginal effects (N_m1=58304) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- age + 1 (centered) | Men | 1 0.072 0.004 0.000 Women | 2 0.017 0.004 0.000 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(intmod, variables = list(age = 1), by = "woman") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output woman Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % Men 0.0720 0.00441 16.32 <0.001 196.4 0.06332 0.0806 Women 0.0167 0.00393 4.26 <0.001 15.6 0.00903 0.0245 Term: age Type: response Comparison: +1 ``` ::: ::: ::: - Easy to test the equality of the marginal effects; in the case of linear effects, will provide equivalent answer to interaction coefficients (but only in this case!) ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . metest 2 - 1 | estimate se pvalue ---------------------------------+-------------------------------- age_woman_1 - age_woman_0 | -0.055 0.006 0.000 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(intmod, variables = list(age = 1), by = "woman", hypothesis = ~ pairwise) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % (Women) - (Men) -0.0552 0.00591 -9.34 <0.001 66.5 -0.0668 -0.0436 Type: response ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **R**: Use **hypothesis** option of **avg_comparisons** :::
